claim: S. pombe and S. cerevisiae Ire1 orthologs share 29% sequence identity.
source: Despite their common role as UPR effectors and conserved domain structures (Figure 1A), S. pombe and S. cerevisiae Ire1 orthologs share 29% sequence identity, and sequence variation may confer Ire1's functional divergence.
evidence: This is a direct statement of measured sequence identity between the two orthologs.

claim: Foreign Ire1s failed to support cell growth of either S. pombe or S. cerevisiae cells when grown on plates containing tunicamycin.
source: However, when grown on plates containing tunicamycin, a drug that blocks N-linked glycosylation and induces ER stress, the foreign Ire1s failed to support cell growth of either S. pombe and S. cerevisiae cells (Figure 1D and E, lanes 3), indicating that S. pombe and S. cerevisiae Ire1s are not interchangeable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E, lanes 3.

claim: S. pombe and S. cerevisiae Ire1s are not interchangeable.
source: However, when grown on plates containing tunicamycin, a drug that blocks N-linked glycosylation and induces ER stress, the foreign Ire1s failed to support cell growth of either S. pombe and S. cerevisiae cells (Figure 1D and E, lanes 3), indicating that S. pombe and S. cerevisiae Ire1s are not interchangeable.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the growth assay data showing failure of cross-species complementation.

claim: The Ire1 lumenal domains have lower sequence identity (21%) than the cytosolic kinase/RNase domains (45%).
source: Since the Ire1 lumenal domains have lower sequence identity (21%) than the cytosolic kinase/RNase domains (45%), we first swapped the Ire1 lumenal domains, generating chimeras with foreign lumenal domains and host species-endogenous transmembrane/cytosolic domains.
evidence: This is a direct statement of measured sequence identities for different domains.

claim: Both chimeras with swapped lumenal domains supported growth on tunicamycin plates.
source: Both chimeras supported growth on tunicamycin plates, suggesting that the divergent Ire1 lumenal domains share a conserved mechanism to sense ER stress and transduce the signal across ER membrane (Figure 1D and E, lanes 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E, lanes 4.

claim: The divergent Ire1 lumenal domains share a conserved mechanism to sense ER stress and transduce the signal across ER membrane.
source: Both chimeras supported growth on tunicamycin plates, suggesting that the divergent Ire1 lumenal domains share a conserved mechanism to sense ER stress and transduce the signal across ER membrane (Figure 1D and E, lanes 4).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the successful complementation by lumenal domain chimeras.

claim: Ire1 chimeras with swapped transmembrane/cytosolic domains failed to restore growth on tunicamycin plates of both S. pombe and S. cerevisiae cells.
source: These Ire1 chimeras failed to restore growth on tunicamycin plates of both S. pombe and S. cerevisiae cells (Figure 1D and E, lanes 5), indicating that the Ire1 transmembrane/cytosolic domains cause the Ire1 functional incompatibility when expressed in the opposing yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E, lanes 5.

claim: The Ire1 transmembrane/cytosolic domains cause the Ire1 functional incompatibility when expressed in the opposing yeast.
source: These Ire1 chimeras failed to restore growth on tunicamycin plates of both S. pombe and S. cerevisiae cells (Figure 1D and E, lanes 5), indicating that the Ire1 transmembrane/cytosolic domains cause the Ire1 functional incompatibility when expressed in the opposing yeast.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the failure of transmembrane/cytosolic domain chimeras to complement.

claim: Only the Ire1 chimera bearing the S. pombe cytosolic domain cleaved the GAS2 mRNA.
source: Of the different Ire1 variants, only the Ire1 chimera bearing the S. pombe cytosolic domain cleaved the GAS2 mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and decreased the mRNA level (Figure 1F), consistent with the growth phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and qPCR data in Figure 1F.

claim: In S. pombe, Ire1 cleaves the BIP1 mRNA within its 3'UTR, producing a truncated mRNA with an increased half-life.
source: In S. pombe, Ire1 also cleaves the BIP1 mRNA within its 3'UTR, producing a truncated mRNA with an increased half-life (Kimmig et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Kimmig et al., 2012.

claim: Ire1 variants bearing the S. pombe cytosolic domain processed BIP1 mRNA, whereas Ire1 variants bearing the S. cerevisiae cytosolic domain did not.
source: As shown in Figure 1G, Ire1 variants bearing the S. pombe cytosolic domain processed BIP1 mRNA, whereas Ire1 variants bearing the S. cerevisiae cytosolic domain did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The two Ire1 constructs bearing the S. pombe cytosolic domains did not splice HAC1 mRNA in S. cerevisiae cells.
source: Consistent with the cell growth phenotype on tunicamycin, the two Ire1 constructs bearing the S. pombe cytosolic domains did not splice HAC1 mRNA in S. cerevisiae cells (Figure 1H, lanes 6, 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H, lanes 6 and 10.

claim: The Ire1 chimera bearing the S. pombe lumenal domain and S. cerevisiae cytosolic domains spliced HAC1 mRNA, albeit at reduced efficiency compared to WT S. cerevisiae Ire1.
source: By contrast, the Ire1 chimera bearing the S. pombe lumenal domain and S. cerevisiae cytosolic domains spliced HAC1 mRNA (Figure 1H, lane 8), albeit at reduced efficiency compared to WT S. cerevisiae Ire1 (Figure 1H, lane 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H, lanes 2 and 8.

claim: The reduced HAC1 mRNA splicing efficiency observed for Ire1 bearing the S. pombe lumenal domain can be explained by the observation that the S. pombe lumenal domain mediates a lower degree of oligomerization than its S. cerevisiae counterpart.
source: The reduced HAC1 mRNA splicing efficiency observed for Ire1 bearing the S. pombe lumenal domain (Figure 1H, lane 8, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, column 4) can be explained by the observation that the S. pombe lumenal domain mediates a lower degree of oligomerization than its S. cerevisiae counterpart, as demonstrated by the reduced ability of Ire1-mCherry fusion constructs to form foci visible by fluorescent microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This explanation is inferred from fluorescence microscopy data showing reduced foci formation in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The S. pombe lumenal domain mediates a lower degree of oligomerization than its S. cerevisiae counterpart.
source: The reduced HAC1 mRNA splicing efficiency observed for Ire1 bearing the S. pombe lumenal domain (Figure 1H, lane 8, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, column 4) can be explained by the observation that the S. pombe lumenal domain mediates a lower degree of oligomerization than its S. cerevisiae counterpart, as demonstrated by the reduced ability of Ire1-mCherry fusion constructs to form foci visible by fluorescent microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The major difference between S. cerevisiae and S. pombe Ire1 lies in the kinase/RNase domains.
source: This result indicates that the major difference lies in the kinase/RNase domains, but that the transmembrane and cytosolic linker domains can afford a marginal rescue, most likely by reintroducing cytosolic linker elements that facilitate HAC1 mRNA docking (van Anken et al., 2014).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental results with various chimeric constructs and supported by citation to van Anken et al., 2014.

claim: The S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase efficiently cleaved a cognate 29-nucleotide RNA hairpin derived from the 3' splice site of S. cerevisiae HAC1 mRNA.
source: The S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase efficiently cleaved a cognate 29-nucleotide RNA hairpin derived from the 3' splice site of S. cerevisiae HAC1 mRNA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro RNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the S. cerevisiae HAC1 mRNA-derived substrate ~60 fold slower than S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase.
source: By contrast, under the same conditions the S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the S. cerevisiae HAC1 mRNA-derived substrate ~60 fold slower (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro RNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase efficiently cleaved a cognate 32-nucleotide RNA hairpin derived from the cleavage site in S. pombe BIP1 mRNA.
source: Reciprocally, the S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase efficiently cleaved a cognate 32-nucleotide RNA hairpin derived from the cleavage site in S. pombe BIP1 mRNA and cognate RNA hairpins derived from the RIDD cleavage sites in S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 and PLB1, whereas S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the BIP1 mRNA-derived substrate and the S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 >500 fold slower and PLB1 mRNA-derived hairpins ~100 fold slower (Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro RNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the BIP1 mRNA-derived substrate >500 fold slower than S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase.
source: Reciprocally, the S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase efficiently cleaved a cognate 32-nucleotide RNA hairpin derived from the cleavage site in S. pombe BIP1 mRNA and cognate RNA hairpins derived from the RIDD cleavage sites in S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 and PLB1, whereas S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the BIP1 mRNA-derived substrate and the S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 >500 fold slower and PLB1 mRNA-derived hairpins ~100 fold slower (Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro RNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 mRNA-derived substrate >500 fold slower than S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase.
source: Reciprocally, the S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase efficiently cleaved a cognate 32-nucleotide RNA hairpin derived from the cleavage site in S. pombe BIP1 mRNA and cognate RNA hairpins derived from the RIDD cleavage sites in S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 and PLB1, whereas S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the BIP1 mRNA-derived substrate and the S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 >500 fold slower and PLB1 mRNA-derived hairpins ~100 fold slower (Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro RNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved PLB1 mRNA-derived hairpins ~100 fold slower than S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase.
source: Reciprocally, the S. pombe Ire1 kinase/RNase efficiently cleaved a cognate 32-nucleotide RNA hairpin derived from the cleavage site in S. pombe BIP1 mRNA and cognate RNA hairpins derived from the RIDD cleavage sites in S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 and PLB1, whereas S. cerevisiae Ire1 kinase/RNase cleaved the BIP1 mRNA-derived substrate and the S. pombe SPAC4G9.15 >500 fold slower and PLB1 mRNA-derived hairpins ~100 fold slower (Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro RNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The different Ire1 RNase specificities separate their functional outputs and are not dependent on other cellular factors such as associated proteins or lipids.
source: These in vitro data validate and expand the conclusions from the experiments conducted in vivo, suggesting that the different Ire1 RNase specificities separate their functional outputs and that they are not dependent on other cellular factors such as associated proteins or lipids.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the in vitro cleavage assay results.

claim: For S. cerevisiae Ire1 a nucleotide sequence of CNG|CNGN or CNG|ANGN situated in a strictly conserved 7-membered loop is required.
source: The required RNA sequence motifs were characterized previously and differ between species: for S. cerevisiae Ire1 a nucleotide sequence of CNG|CNGN or CNG|ANGN ('|' indicates the Ire1 cleavage position) situated in a strictly conserved 7-membered loop is required (Gonzalez et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gonzalez et al., 1999.

claim: For S. pombe Ire1 a three-nucleotide sequence of UG|C is required.
source: By contrast, for S. pombe Ire1 a three-nucleotide sequence of UG|C is required and no additional structural features have yet been characterized (Kimmig et al., 2012; Guydosh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimmig et al., 2012 and Guydosh et al., 2017.

claim: In all 13 additional S. pombe Ire1 substrate mRNA cleavage sites analyzed, cleavage sites were located near the center of loops in RNA stem-loop structures.
source: In similar analyses of 13 additional S. pombe Ire1 substrate mRNA cleavage sites previously identified by both Kimmig, Diaz et al. and Guydosh et al. (Guydosh et al., 2017; Kimmig et al., 2012), we found in all of them cleavage sites located near the center of loops in RNA stem-loop structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DMS modification and RNA structure prediction data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: S. pombe Ire1 is tolerant to loop size variation, while the S. cerevisiae Ire1 stringently recognizes 7-membered stem loops.
source: We summarize that S. pombe Ire1 is tolerant to loop size variation, while the S. cerevisiae Ire1 stringently recognizes 7-membered stem loops.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the analysis of multiple cleavage sites showing variable loop sizes for S. pombe Ire1 substrates.

claim: Both S. cerevisiae and S. pombe Ire1 enzymes cleaved an RNA substrate with sequence CUG|CAGC in a 7-membered stem loop with similar efficiency.
source: Indeed, both enzymes cleaved this RNA in vitro with similar efficiency, in strong support of our model (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: S. pombe Ire1 failed to cleave the BIP1-HAC1 hybrid mRNA upon UPR induction.
source: In support of our model, S. pombe Ire1 failed to cleave the BIP1-HAC1 hybrid mRNA upon UPR induction (Figure 3G, bar 3 and 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3G, bars 3 and 4.

claim: A single nucleotide change from A to U in the BIP1-HAC1 hybrid mRNA restored the S. pombe Ire1 cleavage.
source: Next, we mutated the non-cognate A to a cognate U, such that the S. pombe Ire1 cleavage motif UG|C was restored. Indeed, the single nucleotide change restored the S. pombe Ire1 cleavage (Figure 3G, bar 5 and 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3G, bars 5 and 6.

claim: The Ire1 orthologs in S. cerevisiae and S. pombe have divergent substrate preferences.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the Ire1 orthologs in S. cerevisiae and S. pombe have divergent substrate preferences.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the combined results of sequence motif analysis and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: S. pombe cells contain functional mRNA ligation machinery.
source: To address this question, we tested whether S. pombe cells contain functional mRNA ligation machinery.
evidence: This is tested experimentally by expressing a splicing reporter in S. pombe cells.

claim: Both Ire1 constructs bearing the S. cerevisiae cytosolic domains successfully spliced the reporter mRNA in S. pombe cells.
source: Interestingly, both Ire1 constructs bearing the S. cerevisiae cytosolic domains successfully spliced the reporter mRNA (Figure 4A, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A, lanes 1-4.

claim: The S. pombe cells ligated the mRNA cleavage fragments as long as the correct RNA substrates were provided.
source: Thus, the S. pombe cells ligated the mRNA cleavage fragments as long as the correct RNA substrates were provided.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the successful splicing of the reporter mRNA in S. pombe cells expressing Ire1 with S. cerevisiae cytosolic domains.

claim: Features in the RNA substrates determine their fate post Ire1 cleavage.
source: This result suggested that features in the RNA substrates determine their fate post Ire1 cleavage.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that S. pombe cells can ligate mRNA fragments when provided with appropriate substrates.

claim: The BIP1 mRNA containing the synthetic splicing cassette was spliced in S. pombe upon induction of ER stress.
source: Indeed, we found that the BIP1 mRNA containing the synthetic splicing cassette was spliced in S. pombe upon induction of ER stress (Figure 4C lane 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C, lane 2.

claim: A synthetic mRNA containing the splicing cassette was efficiently spliced in S. pombe upon ER stress.
source: As for the mRNA described above, this construct was efficiently spliced in S. pombe upon ER stress (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The substrate RNA structure determines the fate of the RNA cleavage fragments.
source: Thus, we conclude that the substrate RNA structure determines the fate of the RNA cleavage fragments.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the successful engineering of splicing in S. pombe by introducing appropriate RNA structural elements.

claim: The evolutionary divergence of Ire1's substrate specificity determines the set of mRNAs that are cleaved in either species.
source: Two main conclusions emerged from this study. First, the evolutionary divergence of Ire1's substrate specificity determines the set of mRNAs that are cleaved in either species.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the entire study.

claim: Features in the mRNAs determine the distinct fates of the severed mRNA fragments.
source: Second, features in the mRNAs determine the distinct fates of the severed mRNA fragments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the entire study.

claim: S. pombe can be coopted to carry out the core non-conventional mRNA splicing reaction with fidelity, as long as it is provided with a spliceable RNA substrate that matches the specificity requirements of its endogenous Ire1.
source: S. pombe can be coopted to carry out the core non-conventional mRNA splicing reaction with fidelity, as long as it is provided with a spliceable RNA substrate that matches the specificity requirements of its endogenous Ire1.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the successful engineering of splicing in S. pombe.

claim: No other components (such as the RNA ligase) need to be fundamentally specialized to mediate the core splicing reaction in S. pombe.
source: Albeit not optimized in evolution for efficiency of the reaction, no other components (such as the RNA ligase) need to be fundamentally specialized to mediate the core splicing reaction.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the successful splicing in S. pombe without introducing additional specialized components.

claim: S. pombe Ire1 RNase specificity is more promiscuous, and has a broad substrate scope, in line with its role to initiate degradation of many ER-bound mRNAs to reduce the ER's protein folding burden.
source: S. pombe Ire1 RNase specificity is more promiscuous, and has a broad substrate scope, in line with its role to initiate degradation of many ER-bound mRNAs to reduce the ER's protein folding burden.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observed tolerance to loop size variation and the biological function of S. pombe Ire1.

claim: S. cerevisiae Ire1's RNase specificity is very stringent and specialized with HAC1 mRNA being as its only substrate in the cell.
source: By contrast, S. cerevisiae Ire1's RNase specificity is very stringent and specialized with HAC1 mRNA being as its only substrate in the cell (Niwa et al., 2005), in line with its role to produce a single transcription activator to drive UPR target genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2005 and inference about biological function.

claim: In mammals, two paralogs of Ire1 are expressed in a tissue-specific manner.
source: In mammals, two paralogs of Ire1 are expressed in a tissue-specific manner (Tsuru et al., 2013; Bertolotti et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tsuru et al., 2013 and Bertolotti et al., 2001.

claim: Mammalian Ire1α recognizes a similar but longer RNA sequence motif, CUG|CAG, displayed in stem-loop structures.
source: Ire1α, which performs both XBP1 mRNA splicing and RIDD, recognizes a similar but longer RNA sequence motif, CUG|CAG, displayed in stem-loop structures (Maurel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maurel et al., 2014.

claim: The two cleavage sites on XBP1 mRNA are conserved 7-mer loops.
source: Interestingly, the loop sizes that Ire1α recognizes differ between the XBP1 mRNA cleavage sites and RIDD cleavage sites, with the two cleavage sites on XBP1 mRNA to be conserved 7-mer loops (Hooks and Griffiths-Jones, 2011), while the cleavage sites on RIDD substrates vary in range from 9-mers to 5-mers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hooks and Griffiths-Jones, 2011.

claim: The cleavage sites on RIDD substrates vary in range from 9-mers to 5-mers.
source: Interestingly, the loop sizes that Ire1α recognizes differ between the XBP1 mRNA cleavage sites and RIDD cleavage sites, with the two cleavage sites on XBP1 mRNA to be conserved 7-mer loops (Hooks and Griffiths-Jones, 2011), while the cleavage sites on RIDD substrates vary in range from 9-mers to 5-mers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mammalian Ire1α may display two distinct modes of RNase activity—a more stringent mode of RNase activity observed on 7-mer stem-loop RNAs and a more promiscuous mode of RNase activity on RNA substrates with variable loop sizes.
source: This suggests that mammalian Ire1α may display two distinct modes of RNase activity—a more stringent mode of RNase activity observed on 7-mer stem-loop RNAs (XBP1 mRNA and BLOC1S mRNA) and a more promiscuous mode of RNase activity on RNA substrates with variable loop sizes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion inferred from the observed differences in loop size preferences.

claim: Mammalian Ire1α may switch selectively into one or the other state, perhaps in response to the timing of UPR activation or certain physiological conditions.
source: Hence it seems plausible that mammalian Ire1α may switch selectively into one or the other state, perhaps in response to the timing of UPR activation or certain physiological conditions, which could be reflected in particular oligomeric states, post-translational modifications, or other effectors yet to be discovered.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Ire1α is more efficient in XBP1 mRNA splicing, while Ire1β prefers to cleave ribosomal RNA.
source: Ire1α is more efficient in XBP1 mRNA splicing, while Ire1β prefers to cleave ribosomal RNA (Iwawaki et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 2011; Imagawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iwawaki et al., 2001, Nakamura et al., 2011, and Imagawa et al., 2008.

claim: Two Ire1β cleavage sites both located on rRNA share a common sequence of G|C at the cleavage site.
source: Two Ire1β cleavage sites both located on rRNA, have been mapped to date. They share a common sequence of G|C at the cleavage site.
evidence: This is a statement about previously mapped cleavage sites.

claim: Differences in Ire1α's and Ire1β's RNase domains lead to their functional distinction.
source: Previous studies indicated that differences in Ire1α's and Ire1β's RNase domains lead to their functional distinction (Imagawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Imagawa et al., 2008.

claim: S. pombe Ire1 does not cleave rRNA.
source: We did not observed cleavage of rRNA by S. pombe Ire1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B); mammalian Ire1β's activity to do so may therefore reflect a specialization that is not generalizable to all Ire1 RNases that perform RIDD.
evidence: This claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Modulating Ire1's RNase specificity to regulate its mode of action emerges as a general theme for different species, as well as for different tissues within the same species.
source: Therefore, modulating Ire1's RNase specificity to regulate its mode of action emerges as a general theme for different species, as well as for different tissues within the same species.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the comparative analysis across species and paralogs.

claim: In S. cerevisiae cells, apart from the HAC1 mRNA, other mRNAs contain the S. cerevisiae Ire1 cleavage motif, yet are not cleaved.
source: In S. cerevisiae cells, apart from the HAC1 mRNA, other mRNAs contain the S. cerevisiae Ire1 cleavage motif, yet are not cleaved (Niwa et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2005.

claim: HAC1 mRNA is targeted to Ire1 upon stress, utilizing a specific signal in the HAC1 mRNA 3'UTR.
source: This is explained by spatial coordination. HAC1 mRNA is targeted to Ire1 upon stress, utilizing a specific signal in the HAC1 mRNA 3'UTR (Aragón et al., 2009), conferring exquisite specificity that renders HAC1 mRNA the sole substrate of the reaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aragón et al., 2009.

claim: S. pombe and mammalian cells target XBP1 mRNA and most RIDD substrates to the ER via the signal recognition particle (SRP) pathway.
source: By contrast to the dedicated mRNA targeting in S. cerevisiae, S. pombe and mammalian cells target XBP1 mRNA and most RIDD substrates to the ER via the signal recognition particle (SRP) pathway (Hollien and Weissman, 2006; Hollien et al., 2009; Yanagitani et al., 2009; Yanagitani et al., 2011; Plumb et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hollien and Weissman, 2006; Hollien et al., 2009; Yanagitani et al., 2009; Yanagitani et al., 2011; Plumb et al., 2015.

claim: In mammalian cells where splicing and RIDD co-exist, XBP1 mRNA splicing and RIDD substrate degradation are separated post Ire1 cleavage.
source: After Ire1 cleavage, RNA fragments are ligated or degraded, depending on the substrate RNA structures. According to this notion, in mammalian cells where splicing and RIDD co-exist, we predict that XBP1 mRNA splicing and RIDD substrate degradation are separated post Ire1 cleavage.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings from the study.

claim: The two cleavage sites on the XBP1 mRNA are coordinated by a zipper-like RNA structure, which enable the exons to be held in juxtaposition and ligated by the cytosolic tRNA ligase.
source: The two cleavage sites on the XBP1 mRNA are coordinated by a zipper-like RNA structure, which enable the exons to be held in juxtaposition and ligated by the cytosolic tRNA ligase (Peschek et al., 2015; Sidrauski et al., 1996; Jurkin et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Kosmaczewski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peschek et al., 2015; Sidrauski et al., 1996; Jurkin et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Kosmaczewski et al., 2014.

claim: Cleavage sites on the RIDD substrates lack coordination and the cleavage fragments are further degraded.
source: By contrast, cleavage sites on the RIDD substrates lack such coordination and the cleavage fragments are further degraded.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrast with XBP1 mRNA splicing mechanism.

claim: The ER membrane-resident kinase/RNase Ire1 maintains ER protein homeostasis through two fundamentally distinct processes.
source: The ER membrane-resident kinase/RNase Ire1 maintains ER protein homeostasis through two fundamentally distinct processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about Ire1 function based on established knowledge.

claim: Ire1 can initiate a transcriptional response through a non-conventional mRNA splicing reaction to increase the ER folding capacity.
source: First, Ire1 can initiate a transcriptional response through a non-conventional mRNA splicing reaction to increase the ER folding capacity.
evidence: This is a general statement about Ire1 function based on established knowledge.

claim: Ire1 can decrease the ER folding burden through selective mRNA decay.
source: Second, Ire1 can decrease the ER folding burden through selective mRNA decay.
evidence: This is a general statement about Ire1 function based on established knowledge.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the two Ire1 functions have been evolutionarily separated.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the two Ire1 functions have been evolutionarily separated.
evidence: This is a general statement about the evolutionary divergence of Ire1 functions.

claim: The respective Ire1 orthologs have become specialized for their functional outputs by divergence of their RNase specificities.
source: Here, we show that the respective Ire1 orthologs have become specialized for their functional outputs by divergence of their RNase specificities.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data.

claim: RNA structural features separate the splicing substrates from the decay substrates.
source: In addition, RNA structural features separate the splicing substrates from the decay substrates.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data.

claim: An S. pombe Ire1 cleavage substrate was engineered into a splicing substrate, which confers S. pombe with both Ire1 functional outputs.
source: Using these insights, we engineered an S. pombe Ire1 cleavage substrate into a splicing substrate, which confers S. pombe with both Ire1 functional outputs.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the experimental data.

claim: The most evolutionarily conserved branch of the UPR is mediated by the ER-transmembrane kinase/endoribonuclease (RNase) Ire1.
source: The most evolutionarily conserved branch of the UPR is mediated by the ER-transmembrane kinase/endoribonuclease (RNase) Ire1.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Direct binding of unfolded proteins to Ire1's ER lumenal domain triggers Ire1 to oligomerize and form foci.
source: Direct binding of unfolded proteins to Ire1's ER lumenal domain triggers Ire1 to oligomerize and form foci (Gardner and Walter, 2011; Karagöz et al., 2017; Credle et al., 2005; Aragón et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gardner and Walter, 2011; Karagöz et al., 2017; Credle et al., 2005; Aragón et al., 2009.

claim: Ire1 oligomerization activates Ire1's cytosolic kinase/RNase domain.
source: In turn, Ire1 oligomerization activates Ire1's cytosolic kinase/RNase domain (Korennykh et al., 2009), which restores ER homeostasis through two functional outputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Korennykh et al., 2009.

claim: Translation of the spliced HAC1/XBP1 mRNA produces a transcription factor Xbp1 (Hac1 in S. cerevisiae), which drives a large transcriptional program to adjust the ER's protein-folding capacity according to the protein folding load in the ER lumen.
source: Translation of the spliced mRNA produces a transcription factor Xbp1 (Hac1 in S. cerevisiae), which drives a large transcriptional program to adjust the ER's protein-folding capacity according to the protein folding load in the ER lumen (Cox et al., 1993; Mori et al., 1993; Yoshida et al., 2001; Calfon et al., 2002; Sidrauski et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 1993; Mori et al., 1993; Yoshida et al., 2001; Calfon et al., 2002; Sidrauski et al., 1996.

claim: The initial Ire1-mediated cleavage leads to mRNA degradation, in a process termed regulated Ire1-dependent decay (RIDD).
source: The initial Ire1-mediated cleavage leads to mRNA degradation, in a process termed regulated Ire1-dependent decay (RIDD) (Hollien and Weissman, 2006; Hollien et al., 2009; Kimmig et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hollien and Weissman, 2006; Hollien et al., 2009; Kimmig et al., 2012.

claim: The mechanism that distinguishes the non-conventional mRNA splicing from RIDD has largely remained unknown.
